name: Substance as the persistent subject of predicates
plain_explanation: Later philosophers did not accept Parmenides' extreme claim that nothing at all can change, but they kept a softened version of his idea: that behind changing appearances there must be some persisting 'substance' that stays the same while its properties change.
precise_definition: The concept, which Russell says later philosophy 'accepted from Parmenides' in place of the impossibility of all change, of substance as 'the persistent subject of varying predicates' -- a concept that 'became, and remained for more than two thousand years, one of the fundamental concepts of philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology.'
why_it_mattered: Shows how a refuted philosophical claim (total denial of change) can still leave a lasting, more moderate legacy (belief in persisting substance) that shapes the entire subsequent tradition -- an example, for Russell, of how philosophical refutations are rarely final.
historical_origin: Implicit already in Parmenides' immediate successors, even though the word 'substance' itself does not occur in them.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says he will 'have much to say about it at a later stage', flagging substance as a recurring topic throughout the rest of the book.
